title: k-Nearest Neighbors
hook: The laziest classifier: to label a new point, just find its k closest neighbors in the training set and take a vote - no training required at all.
key_points: No explicit training phase - the entire dataset is the model, stored in memory.
At prediction time, find the k most similar training points (by distance) and aggregate their labels.
k controls the bias-variance tradeoff: small k is flexible and noisy, large k is smooth but coarser.
Prediction is slow on large datasets - computing distances to all training points takes time.
A great sanity-check baseline and a clean way to build intuition about decision boundaries.
content_html: k-Nearest Neighbors (kNN) is about as simple as ML gets: to classify a new example, find the k training points most similar to it, and let them vote. The class with the most votes wins. There is no fitting step - the algorithm just memorizes the training data.
extra_html:
How it works

Similarity is usually measured by Euclidean distance, though other distance functions work too. With k=1 you always label the new point with the class of its single nearest neighbor. Increasing k smooths the decision boundary by consulting more neighbors - reducing sensitivity to noise but making the boundary less flexible. For regression, replace the vote with an average of the neighbors' values.

Why it matters

kNN builds intuition about how local structure in data determines predictions, and it makes the bias-variance tradeoff with k tangible and visual. It is also a useful baseline: if your sophisticated model cannot beat kNN, something is wrong. Its main practical limit is that it scales poorly - prediction time grows with the size of the training set. The Wikipedia article covers variants and distance metrics in more depth.

related.title: k-Means Clustering
related.hook: Pick k cluster centers, assign every point to the nearest one, move each center to the mean of its points, repeat - clusters emerge without any labels.

related.title: Support-Vector Networks (SVMs)
related.hook: An SVM draws the decision boundary that maximizes the gap to the nearest training points - the wider the margin, the better it generalizes to new data.

flashcards.prompt: Why is kNN called a 'lazy' classifier?
flashcards.back_html: There is no training phase - it just memorizes the dataset, then at prediction time finds the k closest points and votes.

flashcards.prompt: How does the choice of k affect kNN's bias-variance tradeoff?

choices.text: Small k is flexible but noisy; large k is smoother but coarser
Small k is smoother; large k is more flexible
k has no effect on the decision boundary

flashcards.explanation_html: Increasing k consults more neighbors, smoothing the boundary and reducing noise sensitivity at the cost of flexibility.

flashcards.prompt: What is kNN's main practical limitation?

choices.text: Prediction is slow - it must compute distances to all training points
It requires a long, expensive training phase
It cannot be used for regression

flashcards.explanation_html: Since the whole dataset is the model, prediction time grows with the training set size. Regression works by averaging neighbors.
